title: Store fuel safely
summary: Keep gasoline out of the house, in approved cans, in a ventilated shed or detached garage away from anything with a flame. Kerosene goes in its own blue can, never a gasoline can. Propane cylinders stay outdoors and upright. Check the heating oil tank, and keep an A-B-C fire extinguisher you know how to use.
doFirst: Never store gasoline in the house (OSHA, American Burn Association).
Keep fuel away from anything with a flame or a pilot light, such as a water heater: gasoline vapor travels along the ground (OSHA, FEMA).
Kerosene only in a can made for kerosene, never in a gasoline can or one that ever held gasoline (CPSC).
Propane cylinders: outdoors, upright, valve closed (North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services).
Fire bigger than one small object, or no clear way out? Get everyone out; don’t fight it (US Fire Administration).

list: Containers: use cans that are listed, labelled or approved for gasoline (American Burn Association; OSHA: approved containers). UL-approved, red for gasoline, labelled, with a spout so you can pour without spilling (Maine Department of Environmental Protection). The newer spill-proof cans are better than old ones (Maine DEP).
Never in glass jars, plastic milk jugs or other makeshift containers (Maine DEP).

Where: outside the house, in a cool, well-ventilated place (American Burn Association), preferably a well-ventilated shed or detached garage, out of children’s reach (Maine DEP). Not an attached garage: Maine names a detached one, and this app reads that strictly. Keep it locked up (American Burn Association). Store fuel away from living areas, never in your home (OSHA).

Away from flames and heat: keep fuel cans away from anything that makes a flame or heat, such as a water heater (OSHA). Gasoline vapor you can’t see can travel along the ground and be lit by a pilot light or a spark from a switch (FEMA).
Away from your well: store gasoline and fuel equipment as far as you can from your drinking water well, and downhill of it (Maine DEP).
Buy only what you will use (Maine DEP).
Check cans, tanks and engines for leaks once a month (Maine DEP).

blocks.p: How much a household may store: no New York limit was found in an opened source.

list: Don’t store gasoline for more than 30 days unless you add a fuel stabilizer, and use a stabilizer made for gasoline that contains ethanol (Maine DEP).
If you store gasoline over the winter or for more than a month, keep the can or tank 95 percent full (Maine DEP).
Old plain gasoline (not two-stroke gas and oil mix) can be used up in a car, mixed 1 part old to 5 parts fresh (Maine DEP). Otherwise take it to a household hazardous waste collection (Maine DEP).
Never mix leftover two-stroke gas and oil with used engine oil (Maine DEP).

blocks.p: Only one opened source, Maine’s environmental agency, gives a storage time. No federal or New York source opened gives one.

list: Use gasoline outdoors only (American Burn Association).
Fill engines only when they are cool (American Burn Association). Turn a generator off and let it cool before refuelling (OSHA, FEMA).
Never fill a can while it sits inside a vehicle or in a pickup truck bed (American Burn Association).
Never siphon gasoline by mouth (American Burn Association).
Never use gasoline near a flame, to start a fire or to burn brush, or as a cleaning fluid or solvent (American Burn Association; Maine DEP).
Never put gasoline in a kerosene heater (CPSC).

Keep it in its own container made for kerosene, never in a gasoline can or a can that has ever held gasoline (CPSC). Store kerosene away from other fuel containers (CPSC). Kerosene cans are usually blue and gasoline cans red (CPSC; Maine DEP: blue for kerosene and diesel).
Store it outdoors, in a container used only for kerosene (New York State Department of Health).
Even a little gasoline mixed into kerosene can cause a fire or explosion in a heater (CPSC).
Buy water-clear 1-K kerosene from a dealer who can certify it is 1-K (CPSC). Don’t burn kerosene left from last heating season (New York State Department of Health).
Store every cylinder that holds or has held propane outdoors (North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, LP-Gas Section).

Never indoors, and never under the house or in a crawlspace (North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services). Don’t bring cylinders into the house or into a garage or basement (National Propane Gas Association).
Stand them upright on the foot ring, never on their side or upside down (North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services).

Check that the valve closes completely, then close it before storing (North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services; National Propane Gas Association). On a disconnected tank with an older valve that has only inside threads, screw in a plug; never put a plug in a valve with outside threads (Acme), which disables a safety feature (North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services).

Keep them away from flames and anything that could light them, out of hot sun, and where they can’t fall or be knocked over by children (North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services).
Keep spare cylinders away from a grill that is in use (North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services; National Propane Gas Association).
Don’t leave a cylinder in a vehicle (National Propane Gas Association).

One exception, while a heater is in use (Kerosene and propane heaters): indoors, only a 1 lb. cylinder screwed onto the heater. Never a 20 lb. (grill-size) or larger tank inside the house or garage, and never one brought in on a hose or a hose run into the house from a tank outside (this app’s reading of the 1 lb. rule). Empty cylinders go back outside too. CPSC’s indoor-use standard covers only heaters on 1 lb. cylinders. Minnesota’s State Fire Marshal, reading the national propane code (NFPA 58), allows no cylinder over 1 lb. and no more than 2 lb. in all inside a home, garages included, counts a connected cylinder as in use and an empty one as full. That is another state’s reading, used here as guidance.

blocks.p: The North Carolina rules are that state’s law, used here as guidance. No current New York rule on storing propane cylinders at home was found in an opened source.
New York State Department of Environmental Conservation says to check the tank before you order oil, and to have it inspected every year.

list: Above-ground tank: look for bent, rusty or wobbly legs or an unstable base; rust, weeps, wet spots or many dents; drips at the filter or valves; oil lines without a protective casing; eaves where snow and ice could fall on the tank; stains or a strong oil smell on the ground; plants dying around it (DEC).
Make sure snow, ice or insect nests are not blocking the tank vent, and look for spills around the fill and vent pipes (DEC).
Look for a cracked, stuck or frozen fuel gauge, or fuel around it (DEC).
Ask the delivery driver whether the overfill whistle sounded (a silent whistle is a warning sign) and whether the vent pipe is the right size (DEC).
Buried tank: water in the tank, oil or a sheen in the basement sump, odd tastes or smells in well water, neighbors smelling oil, or using more oil than normal are warning signs (DEC).
If you see any of these, contact your oil service company (DEC). Report oil spills or leaks to the DEC Spills Hotline, 1-800-457-7362 (DEC).

blocks.p: Keep a multipurpose A-B-C extinguisher. Multipurpose extinguishers work on most home fires; A-B-C also covers ordinary materials such as wood, paper and cloth (A), as well as burning liquids such as gasoline and oil (B) and plugged-in electrical equipment (C) (US Fire Administration). A B-C unit does not cover class A. Get one with a UL or ULC Listed label, the largest you can handle easily, and keep it where nothing blocks your way to it (US Fire Administration).

blocks.warn: Use it only if everyone else has been warned, the fire department has been called, the fire is small and in one object or surface, you are able to use it, you are protected from the smoke, and you have a clear way out. Otherwise get out (US Fire Administration). Young children and older adults should not use one (US Fire Administration).

steps: Pull the pin, with the nozzle pointing away from you (US Fire Administration).
Aim low, at the base of the fire (US Fire Administration).
Squeeze the lever slowly and evenly (US Fire Administration).
Sweep the nozzle from side to side (US Fire Administration).

blocks.p: Check the pressure gauge, and look for dents, rust or damage to the can, hose and nozzle. Follow the maker’s instructions: some must be shaken monthly, and some replaced if the pressure is low (US Fire Administration).
